transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-20 16:00 UTC / Duration 48m / Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Lopez (CrimsonBay CTO), Ravi Kumar (Lead ML), Elena Park (Infra PM)

Summary:
- CrimsonBay is building a live chat assistant for tradeshow launch with 5000 concurrent users potential at peak; target p95 for streaming answer latency <= 350ms for short responses (<=150 tokens) and <= 700ms for long form (>=600 tokens). Interested in Redwood Hosted to start but wants predictability for burst windows.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming token/sec, burst sizing, KV cache, Dedicated vs Hosted, SOC2/KMS.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros? We'll do a short product framing then jump into your traffic and SLOs.
[00:12] Sofia (CrimsonBay): Hi, Sofia here, CTO. We have Ravi and Elena with me. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:18] Maya: Awesome. Devon, do you want to intro yourself?
[00:21] Devon (Redwood SE): Yeah hi, I'm Devon, I run performance and deployment assists — I can dig into batching, streaming behavior, and the benchmark plan.
[00:27] Ravi: Quick context, our app is a live product recommender with multi-turn clarifying questions. We're expecting a launch event where traffic could spike and we need to hit p95 on streaming responses.
[00:36] Elena: From infra, we're responsible for SSO, network egress, and we need to understand what network footprints Redwood has for Hosted vs Dedicated.
[00:45] Maya: Great. Can you give ballpark numbers for steady-state and peak?
[00:50] Sofia: Steady is about 200 concurrent users, peaks could be 3k-5k concurrent for a 20-minute promo, average response length ~120 tokens; sometimes we have follow-ups up to 900 tokens.
[01:05] Devon: Ok that's helpful. Are you planning streaming partial token streaming to the client?
[01:08] Ravi: Yes, streaming; we need low tail latency for the first token and steady throughput for the rest.
[01:16] Devon: Two things to think about: p95 for first-byte is often dominated by scheduling and token emission; p95 for full response depends on tokens/sec and batching. We typically measure both p95 start-of-stream and p95 completion.
[01:30] Maya: What are your SLO targets? You mentioned earlier 350ms p95 for short responses?
[01:34] Sofia: Right, for responses <150 tokens we want <=350ms p95 start-to-first-chunk and <=700ms p95 end-to-end. For the long ones we'll accept up to 1.2s p95 end-to-end but want predictable cost.
[01:47] Devon: OK, so plan A: Redwood Hosted with suggested batching and KV cache enabled to reduce token compute for recommendations. Plan B: Dedicated pool with burst capacity for the event window.
[01:58] Ravi: How does KV cache work with streaming? Any cold-start penalties?
[02:02] Devon: The KV cache (some folks call it K V cash in docs) stores recent key/value states. For streaming, the first invocation may still incur some kernel latency if the model segment is cold, but for repeated prompts during surge the cache helps reduce compute per token significantly. Cold start is more about model load time and memory warming — with Dedicated you can keep model resident which cuts cold start out.
[02:22] Elena: Any notes on model residency and pre-warming? We need to ensure startup under 2s during the promo.
[02:27] Devon: With Dedicated you can pin model versions and dedicate GPUs; warm startup between requests is subsecond ordinarily. For Hosted, we offer reserved capacity bursts that you can prebook — it's generally faster than on-demand but not as deterministic as pinned Dedicated GPUs.
[02:41] Maya: Let's talk numbers — tokens/sec and worker counts. Ravi, what distribution of request lengths do you have?
[02:46] Ravi: Most are short: 70% under 150 tokens, 20% 150-400, 10% long threads. During the promo the rate of new conversations will spike — so concurrency increases more than tokens per conv.
[02:58] Devon: For a target p95 start-of-stream <=350ms at 3k concurrency, we'll aim for a worker capacity that offers ~X tokens/sec per GPU (Devon laughs), rough rule of thumb: on our optimized runtime a single high-end GPU can sustain ~12k tokens/sec for short-chat workloads if quantized. But that's super workload dependent.
[03:18] Ravi: When you say quantized, are you referring to INT8 paths? We plan to keep quality high, can we use bfloat16?
[03:25] Devon: Yes, we support multiple execution modes. INT8/4 reduces cost but may impact output quality for some instruction-heavy prompts. bfloat16 is the safe middle ground and common for production quality. We'll profile your prompts to recommend a quantization profile.
[03:36] Sofia: How do we model burst capacity billing? We don't want a massive bill for a 20-minute spike.
[03:41] Maya: We have burst pricing options for Hosted, and for Dedicated you can have baseline reserved capacity plus short-term burst credits. We'll send a worksheet that models cost for a 20-minute 5k-concurrency spike vs keeping Dedicated all the time.
[03:54] Elena: Also need to confirm network egress and data residency for logs and traces. We are regulated, so audit logs need to be stored in our region.
[04:02] Devon: For Hosted we support region pinning to AWS regions and can integrate with customer KMS for encryption-at-rest of payloads in Dedicated/Private deployments. Audit logs are exportable to your SIEM via S3 or syslog.
[04:16] Ravi: Are there SOC2 / ISO docs we can review?
[04:19] Maya: Yes, we'll share our security pack. It includes SOC2 Type II, ISO statement, and SSO/SAML integration patterns.
[04:25] Sofia: One big concern — consistency of streaming p95 under backpressure. If tokens/sec spikes, does Redwood shed load or queue? We need graceful degradation, not long tails.
[04:36] Devon: We have smart routing and backpressure policies. For Hosted, we can set a per-tenant concurrency cap and fall back to a smaller model variant or queue with early rejection. For Dedicated you can set burst policies with autoscaling and graceful throttles. We can simulate your token arrival pattern in the benchmark to see the tail behavior.
[04:54] Maya: Could we run a simple benchmark during the pilot to emulate the 20-minute spike and measure p95 for both start and completion, for streaming and non-streaming?
[05:02] Ravi: That would be ideal. We have historical logs from a smaller test launch — we'll share.
[05:07] Devon: I'll spin up a harness that replays your request rate and prompt distribution against a hosted sandbox and against a dedicated reserved pool. Expect a results doc with p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec profiles.
[05:18] Elena: What's the timeline to get sandbox results?
[05:21] Devon: If you share the prompt set and logs by Tue (2025-04-21) I can run initial runs by Fri (2025-04-25).
[05:27] Sofia: Sounds good.
[05:30] (brief crosstalk)
[05:36] Ravi: Also curious about streaming chunk size — we want early partial answers; does chunk size affect p95 markedly?
[05:42] Devon: Yes, chunking and how you set the emission window affects client-perceived latency. Smaller chunks reduce first-byte latency but slightly increase compute overhead. We'll recommend chunk tuning in the profiling.
[05:56] Maya: Any legal / procurement items we should flag now?
[06:00] Elena: We'll need standard DPA, security questionnaire answers, and a data flow diagram. If we go Dedicated/Private we'll likely require a BAA later.
[06:10] Maya: We'll include DPA and security pack. For Dedicated deployments we have an enterprise package that includes a BAA addendum.
[06:17] Devon: Technical note — for Dedicated model pinning we can do warm standby nodes in the same region to reduce failover time. For multi-region failover there is a slight penalty in start-of-stream but it's managed by our routing layer.
[06:31] Ravi: If we do dedicated, can we control quantization policy? We need to be able to run custom quant flags.
[06:36] Devon: Yes, in Dedicated/Private you get more levers; we can run custom kernel flags and quant profiles. Hosted offers curated quant profiles but not custom kernel flags.
[06:47] Sofia: One more question: we use internal embeddings for reranking; can embeddings be generated in the same pipeline or do you recommend separate endpoints?
[06:54] Devon: We recommend separating heavy embedding generation into batch jobs or a dedicated endpoint to avoid impacting streaming chat latency. But it's configurable. We'll show tradeoffs in the runbook.
[07:05] Maya: Let's sketch the acceptance criteria — what would success look like for CrimsonBay after the pilot?
[07:10] Sofia: Pilot shows p95 start <=350ms for short responses during the 20-minute spike at 3k concurrency and end-to-end <=700ms for typical responses. Also a cost model that keeps incremental cost for the spike under 3x steady-state. Security pack accepted.
[07:23] Maya: Great, we'll aim for that.
[07:25] (silence)
[07:32] Devon: Quick clarifying — is the client expecting server-sent events or websocket streaming?
[07:36] Ravi: Websocket.
[07:39] Devon: Good. We'll include websocket binary framing guidance and suggestions for chunk size and backpressure handling.
[07:47] Sofia: Any hard limits on concurrent websocket connections per tenant?
[07:51] Maya: Hosted has soft limits by default but can be raised; Dedicated you control capacity. We'll note recommended caps in the worksheet.
[07:59] Elena: On logs — we want tracing down to token emission to correlate errors with upstream services. Is that possible?
[08:05] Devon: We emit token-level traces that can be exported; sampling may be applied in Hosted to control volume, but Dedicated can have full retention.
[08:16] Ravi: Excellent.
[08:19] Maya: Anything else?
[08:21] Sofia: Procurement wants an estimate for a weekend-long test as well. Might ask to simulate 8-hour sustained moderate load.
[08:28] Maya: We'll include that scenario in the cost worksheet.
[08:32] Devon: On the benchmark side, I'll include p50/p95/p99 curves, tokens/sec over time, CPU/GPU util during the spike, and emitter timings. We'll also compare Hosted and Dedicated numeric results.
[08:45] Ravi: One gotcha — our tokenization is slightly different because we include a lot of product metadata; could that skew tokens/sec?
[08:51] Devon: Yes, we'll tokenize with your exact tokenizer in the harness so numbers are accurate. If you have a custom tokenizer pack send it.
[08:59] Maya: Ok recap and next steps: we'll send pricing and security pack; Devon will run benchmark if prompt set and logs arrive by Tue; schedule pilot kickoff week of Apr 28.
[09:12] Sofia: Agreed.
[09:14] Elena: Thanks everyone.
[09:17] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcription quality: a few terms may be mistranscribed (K V cache, quan-tization), some speaker labels generalized.
